prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "CRWD" (ticker CRWD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "CRWD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc.
markets: Next-gen SIEM and security log management
Managed detection and response and threat intelligence

mission.statement: We are on a mission to protect our customers from breaches
mission.plain: Stop hackers from breaking into the companies and governments that rely on it.

about.plain: CrowdStrike makes software that guards computers, servers and cloud accounts against hackers. A small program called Falcon runs on each computer and sends what it sees to CrowdStrike's cloud, where AI and human experts spot attacks and stop them. Companies pay a yearly subscription and can switch on more protection modules as they need them. It also has a team that helps companies clean up after a break-in.
about.customers: Businesses of all sizes and governments that need to protect their computers, cloud systems and employee logins from hackers.
about.everyday: If your bank, hospital or airline keeps your data safe from hackers, there is a good chance CrowdStrike's software is running on its computers; it was also the company behind the July 2024 update that crashed about 8.5 million Windows PCs and grounded flights worldwide.

money.plain: Falcon protection for laptops, servers, cloud and logins, paid yearly
Experts who investigate and clean up breaches
Collecting and searching a company's security logs to find attacks
A pay-as-you-go plan that lets customers try and add any module

money.part: AI security and Charlotte AI agents
money.plain: AI helpers that run security work and protection for companies' own AI tools

result.summary: CrowdStrike has a real and widening moat: one lightweight agent and a single cloud platform that sees trillions of security events a week, so each new module is easy to add and hard to rip out. Customers keep buying more (51% of subscription customers used six or more modules in Q2 FY2027) and ending ARR reached $5.84 billion, up 25%, despite the July 2024 outage. Its main limits are Microsoft bundling Defender into enterprise licences and Palo Alto Networks' broad platform push, plus continuing GAAP operating losses driven by stock compensation.

pricingPower.evidence: Customers pay premium subscription prices and keep adding modules (Falcon Flex accounts' ending ARR passed $2.29 billion in Q2 FY2027, up 101%), and subscription GAAP gross margin is about 78%; but after the July 2024 outage CrowdStrike gave affected customers 'customer commitment packages' (extra modules, discounts, extended terms) that slowed revenue, and Microsoft's bundled Defender limits how far it can raise list prices.

moats.evidence: CrowdStrike and its Falcon brand are widely seen as the gold standard in endpoint detection, a Leader in Gartner's Endpoint Protection Magic Quadrant for many consecutive reports, and its threat-intelligence work (naming groups like Fancy Bear) is widely cited; the July 2024 outage dented but did not break the brand, as ARR kept growing.

Falcon's agent sits on every endpoint and feeds security operations workflows; once customers run six or more modules (51% do) on one console, replacing it means redeploying agents and retraining staff, and dollar-based gross and net retention rose in Q2 FY2027.

Its Threat Graph learns from telemetry across tens of thousands of customers, so an attack seen at one customer improves detection for all; this is a data network effect rather than a direct user-to-user one.

A single lightweight agent and multi-tenant cloud let it add modules at little extra cost, producing $1.24 billion of free cash flow on $4.81 billion of FY2026 revenue; Microsoft, however, has far greater scale.
Enterprise security is a large market with several well-funded rivals (Microsoft, Palo Alto Networks, SentinelOne), so it does not support only one or two players.

As a cloud-native, AI-first company it counter-positioned against on-premise antivirus vendors such as Symantec and McAfee, who struggled to move off signature-based products without hurting their existing business; that edge is now fading as rivals have also moved to the cloud.
Its threat hunting (OverWatch), incident response and intelligence teams have years of know-how from investigating major breaches, which feeds detection models that are hard to copy quickly.

It holds a large proprietary dataset of security telemetry and threat intelligence on hundreds of adversary groups, plus experienced security researchers, but it has no exclusive licence or legal monopoly.

customers.evidence: Customer loyalty held up through the July 2024 outage: ending ARR grew to $5.25 billion in FY2026 and $5.84 billion in Q2 FY2027 (up 25%), net new ARR hit a record $332.8 million that quarter, and the company said dollar-based gross and net retention rates increased.

talent.evidence: CrowdStrike is a magnet for security researchers thanks to its threat-intelligence reputation and remote-first culture, and it has appeared on Fortune and Great Place to Work 'best workplace' lists; heavy stock compensation (a key reason for its GAAP losses) helps it keep staff.

product.evidence: Falcon is consistently rated a Leader in Gartner's Endpoint Protection Platforms Magic Quadrant and scores at the top of MITRE ATT&CK enterprise evaluations; it has expanded from endpoint into cloud, identity, Next-Gen SIEM and Charlotte AI on one agent, though the July 2024 faulty update showed the risk of its deep kernel-level access.

competitors.name: Microsoft
competitors.note: Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Cloud, Entra identity and Sentinel SIEM, often bundled in Microsoft 365 E5 licences

competitors.name: Palo Alto Networks
competitors.note: Cortex XDR/XSIAM, Prisma Cloud (Cortex Cloud) and CyberArk identity security; the main rival platform

competitors.name: SentinelOne
competitors.note: Singularity endpoint, cloud and AI SIEM platform, the closest pure-play rival

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Cloud Security, Mandiant, Wiz)
competitors.note: Google Security Operations SIEM, Mandiant incident response and threat intelligence, and Wiz cloud security

competitors.name: Fortinet
competitors.note: FortiEDR, FortiSIEM and SecOps bundled with its firewall-centred platform

competitors.name: Zscaler
competitors.note: Zero-trust access, data security and its Red Canary MDR and security operations push; also a CrowdStrike partner

competitors.name: Cisco Systems (Splunk)
competitors.note: Splunk SIEM, Cisco XDR and Secure Endpoint

competitors.name: Trend Micro
competitors.note: Endpoint and cloud workload protection (Vision One)

competitors.name: Sophos
competitors.note: Endpoint and managed detection and response for mid-market firms; owns Secureworks

competitors.name: Arctic Wolf
competitors.note: Managed detection and response (security operations as a service)

competitors.name: Okta
competitors.note: Identity security, where CrowdStrike sells identity threat protection

competitors.name: Broadcom (Symantec Enterprise)
competitors.note: Symantec Endpoint Security for large legacy enterprise customers

competitors.name: Rapid7
competitors.note: SIEM, vulnerability management and MDR for mid-market

competitors.name: Trellix
competitors.note: Legacy McAfee/FireEye endpoint and XDR customers

marketShare.measure: revenue (IDC; latest = calendar 2024, earlier = July 2021-June 2022; CrowdStrike's 2024 share not published in sources checked)

threats: Microsoft bundling Defender, Sentinel and Entra into E5 licences at little extra cost, especially for budget-constrained customers
Platform consolidation by Palo Alto Networks (now including CyberArk) and Google (Mandiant plus Wiz) competing for the same 'single security platform' budget
Another faulty update like the July 19, 2024 incident, which crashed about 8.5 million Windows devices and led to lawsuits (including from Delta Air Lines) and customer concessions
Microsoft moving security vendors out of the Windows kernel, which could narrow the technical gap between Falcon and Defender
Persistent GAAP operating losses (-6.1% operating margin in FY2026) from heavy stock-based compensation diluting shareholders
AI-native start-ups and agentic security tools resetting how security operations are bought
Slower IT budgets or price competition squeezing the premium it charges

ceo.name: George Kurtz
ceo.background: Accountant by training (Seton Hall University BS in accounting, former CPA); founded Foundstone, then worldwide CTO of McAfee before co-founding CrowdStrike

c1.evidence: CrowdStrike pioneered cloud-native endpoint detection and is a leader of the fast-growing cloud security platform market, with ending ARR of $5.84 billion in Q2 FY2027, up 25% year over year.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Falcon for detection quality, one lightweight agent and a single console for endpoint, cloud, identity and SIEM, an advantage built on 15 years of threat data that has proved durable even after the July 2024 outage.

c3.evidence: CrowdStrike is the default name in enterprise endpoint security and became broadly known to the public after the July 2024 outage, but ordinary consumers do not use its products and Microsoft holds the larger IDC market share (28.6% in 2024).

c4.evidence: Its stated mission, 'to protect our customers from breaches', is repeated in nearly every earnings call and keynote, and stopping state-backed and criminal hackers for a decade clearly matters to hospitals, governments and businesses.

c6.evidence: “cybersecurity leader, Falcon, the Windows outage” - among business and tech audiences the impression is mostly positive and strong, but many ordinary people first remember the July 2024 global IT outage, so the public view is mixed.

c7.evidence: CrowdStrike sells into a very large, growing cybersecurity market spanning endpoint, cloud, identity, SIEM and AI security, which it describes as a total addressable market of hundreds of billions of dollars, riding secular trends of cloud migration, AI-powered attacks and vendor consolidation.

c8.evidence: It has expanded from endpoint into cloud security, identity, Next-Gen SIEM, exposure management, data protection and AI agent security, all on the same Falcon agent and platform.

m1.evidence: George Kurtz founded CrowdStrike in 2011 on the then-contrarian vision of a cloud-native, AI-driven security platform replacing signature antivirus, and now pitches an 'agentic security' future with Charlotte AI.

m2.evidence: Kurtz co-founded the company in 2011, has led it for about 15 years and still owns a large stake, consistently prioritising long-term platform investment over GAAP profit.

m4.evidence: Kurtz emphasises 'customer obsession' and personally apologised and offered customer commitment packages after the July 2024 incident, but there is little independent evidence of an unusually servant-style leadership approach.

m5.evidence: He built a remote-first, mission-driven culture of threat hunters and engineers that has launched many modules (cloud, identity, Next-Gen SIEM, Charlotte AI, Falcon Flex) in a few years.

m6.evidence: Kurtz is a hands-on security technologist who co-wrote 'Hacking Exposed' and was CTO of McAfee, though his formal training is in accounting rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: Kurtz frames the work as protecting society from cybercrime and nation-state attacks, but there is no strong public record of causes beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No record was found of George Kurtz giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Kurtz is recognisable as a racing driver (he competes in endurance races such as the 24 Hours of Le Mans) and outspoken industry figure, but he is not a pop-culture personality like Elon Musk.

m9.evidence: Under Kurtz revenue grew from $1.45 billion in FY2022 to $4.81 billion in FY2026, with FY2026 free cash flow of $1.24 billion, and net new ARR reached a record $332.8 million in Q2 FY2027 after the 2024 outage.

m10.evidence: There is no particular reputation for frugality; the company spends heavily on stock compensation, marketing (Fal.Con, Formula 1 sponsorship) and sales.

c10.evidence: Its software protects the computers of thousands of hospitals, banks, airlines and governments, indirectly safeguarding billions of people's data, but it does not improve daily lives directly the way search or streaming do.

p2.evidence: Detecting and stopping sophisticated, constantly changing attacks in real time across millions of devices is extremely hard and is vital to keeping hospitals, power grids and banks running.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew every year: $1.45 billion (FY2022), $2.24 billion (FY2023), $3.95 billion (FY2025) and $4.81 billion (FY2026), with $1.47 billion in Q2 FY2027 alone.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin has stayed around 75% (74.7% in FY2026) and the GAAP operating margin fell from -2.9% in FY2025 to -6.1% in FY2026, so margins have not risen steadily.

f3.evidence: At January 31, 2026 it held $5.23 billion of cash against $745 million of long-term debt, generated $1.24 billion of free cash flow in FY2026, and has positive shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $941 million in FY2023 to $1.61 billion in FY2026, but GAAP operating loss widened to $293 million in FY2026 from $116 million in FY2025.

v1.evidence: Falcon is widely rated best in class for detection (Gartner Leader, top MITRE scores) and runs everything on one agent, but Microsoft Defender is 'good enough' and nearly free for many E5 customers, so it is not the obvious choice for everyone.

v2.evidence: CrowdStrike has appeared on Fortune and Great Place to Work 'best workplace' lists, but it is not ranked among the very top employers like Google or NVIDIA.

c5.evidence: Thousands of hospitals, banks, airlines and governments would immediately lose protection against ransomware and nation-state hackers, as the July 2024 outage showed how deeply its software is embedded in critical systems.
